newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuelan tugs to try to refloat stricken dredger.
newsitem.headline: Venezuelan tugs to try to refloat stricken dredger.

text.p: Venezuelan shipping authorities will try to refloat a grounded dredger blocking the country's main oil export route at 1600 local time/2000 GMT, shipping agents said on Tuesday.
The Lake Maracaibo shipping channel which exports over a million barrels per day of crude oil was closed at 2210 local/0210 GMT last night when the Catatumbo went aground between buoys 24 and 26.

"They are going to try and refloat her at 1600 hours," a shipping agent in Maracaibo said. He said Venezuelan tugs would attempt to push the dredger off a shallow bank in the channel as the tide was rising.

The National Dredging Institute (INC) declined to comment on the grounding of its dredger, but agents said the ship had probably grounded on purpose to avoid losing the whole ship after water was found leaking into the pump room.
The grounding is the latest in a spate of accidents in the narrow strech of water linking Venezuela's most productive oilfields and their world markets.

It hit the headlines in February when the Greek-flagged Nissos Amorgos tanker went aground spilling 25,000 barrels of crude. Since then, several other oil tankers have scraped the silty channel floor, and some run aground, but there have been no more spills.
"The Catatumbo went aground in the same spot as the accident," an agent said.
The INC president was sacked in March over the Nissos fiasco, but shippers say the silting problem has worsened since then.
The Maracaibo port captain cut the maximum draught from 39 foot six inches to 37 foot three inches, and many major shipping companies are using a 36 foot maximum.
Only last week, Venezuela's state-owned oil company Petroleos de Venezuela (PDVSA) instructed its own fleet not to load beyond 36 feet draught after one of its ships nearly went aground at 37 foot.

The reduced draught means tankers load about 70,000 barrels less oil in each ship than normal. Exports have been maintained by topping-up tankers in terminals in the Caribbean before heading to their destination.
